opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the place where a dataflow architecture really shines is anywhere you have large models with a lot of data movement, where the bottleneck isn't raw compute but getting data to the compute efficiently. The most obvious one right now is large language models, both training and especially inference. When you're serving these big models, you want to keep the weights and activations on chip as much as possible and avoid the round trips to off-chip memory that you get with a kernel-by-kernel execution model. With a reconfigurable dataflow approach, you can map a whole chunk of the model spatially across the chip and pipeline the computation, so you get much better utilization and much lower latency.

Beyond language models, we're seeing a lot of interest in things like high-resolution computer vision. Think of medical imaging or satellite imagery, where the images are so large that on a conventional GPU you have to tile them down or reduce the resolution, and you lose accuracy. Because we have a lot of on-chip and attached memory, you can train on the full-resolution images directly, and that turns out to matter quite a bit for accuracy.

Recommendation systems are another big one. They have these huge embedding tables and very sparse, irregular access patterns, which conventional architectures don't handle that well. Having lots of memory capacity close to the compute, plus the flexibility to handle sparse operations, makes a real difference there.

And then there's the scientific computing side: people combining traditional simulation with machine learning, physics-informed models, things like that. Those workloads tend not to look like a neat sequence of dense matrix multiplies, and that's exactly where flexibility in the hardware pays off.

So the common thread is this: as models get bigger and more varied, and as people want to deploy them in production rather than just run benchmarks, the efficiency of data movement becomes the key issue. That's really what we designed the architecture around.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the architecture we've built at SambaNova is what we call a reconfigurable dataflow architecture, and the key idea is that instead of forcing a computation through a fixed pipeline of instructions the way a CPU or a GPU does, you map the dataflow graph of the application directly onto the hardware. The compute and memory are laid out spatially to match the structure of the problem. So the use cases that really come to the fore are the ones where that structure matters most.

The first and most obvious one is training and inference for very large models, the big transformer-based language models. These models are so large that you quickly run into limits on a GPU with memory capacity and with the overhead of moving data on and off the chip. With dataflow, we can keep more of the model and the intermediate activations on-chip, fuse layers together, and avoid the constant round trips to memory. That translates into better performance per chip and, maybe more importantly, the ability to run models that wouldn't otherwise fit without a lot of painful partitioning.

The second area is what I'd call high-resolution or large-input problems. Think about medical imaging, where you have a pathology slide that might be a hundred thousand pixels on a side, or satellite imagery, or scientific data from a telescope or a simulation. Today people chop those images into tiles because the hardware can't handle the full image, and you lose context when you do that. A dataflow architecture lets you process at native resolution, so the model actually sees the whole picture.

A third one is recommendation systems, which are economically probably the most important deep learning workload out there. Those have enormous embedding tables, terabytes in some cases, and the access pattern is sparse and irregular. GPUs are really not well suited to that; it's more of a memory problem than a compute problem. Having a large pool of memory tightly coupled to the compute and being able to express that sparse access as part of the dataflow is a big win.

And then the thing I'm personally very excited about is the convergence of AI and traditional high-performance computing. Scientists are starting to use neural networks as surrogates inside simulations, or to drive experiments in real time. Those workloads mix dense linear algebra, sparse operations, and learned components, and because the architecture is reconfigurable you can express all of that in one graph rather than bouncing between different kinds of hardware.

What ties all of these together is that they are workloads where the limiting factor isn't raw FLOPS, it's data movement. And that's exactly what dataflow is designed to address.

astra-6.text:
I think the use cases that are particularly interesting are the ones where you have very large amounts of data and you want to do more sophisticated learning on that data. Natural language processing is a good example, as are recommendation systems. In both cases, you want to capture richer relationships, and that puts demands on both computation and memory.

The opportunity for our architecture is to organize the computation and the movement of data together. Rather than spending so much energy moving data back and forth, you keep it close to where it’s being used and let it flow through the computation. That opens up possibilities for larger models, but also for making existing applications more efficient.

And ultimately, what’s exciting is giving people the flexibility to explore models they couldn’t practically run before.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most compelling use cases are those where you need to bring together different types of computation. In an AI application, you’re not just running a neural network. You’re preparing data, running the model, and then doing something with the result. The opportunity for our architecture is to make that whole application efficient, rather than accelerating just one piece of it.

Recommendation systems are a good example, because they combine learning with a lot of data movement and irregular access patterns. More broadly, I’m interested in applications where the models and algorithms are still evolving. You want an architecture that can adapt as those workloads change, while still delivering the efficiency you need to run them at scale.
